title: From Chaturanga to Chess
text: Most historians trace chess to an Indian game called chaturanga, played by about the sixth century. Forms of the game traveled through Persia and the Islamic world into Europe. Rules changed along the way. Chess history is therefore a history of exchange, adaptation, and many cultures adding ideas.
context: A cautious summary of the leading scholarly account of chess origins.
vocabulary: adaptation: change for a new use

title: The Queen Changes the Game
text: In late medieval Europe, chess rules changed so the queen and bishop could move much farther. The faster game rewarded development, king safety, and calculation. Historians sometimes call it mad queen chess. A small rule change transformed strategy, showing how systems can produce new behavior when one condition changes.
context: A summary of major chess-rule changes around the late fifteenth century.
vocabulary: development: bringing pieces into useful play

title: Pawns Are the Soul
text: François-André Danican Philidor argued that pawns shape the plan of a chess game. Because pawns usually cannot move backward, each advance changes the position permanently. Strong players ask what squares a pawn move controls, what it weakens, and whether the resulting structure will help later pieces.
context: An explanation of Philidor's influential eighteenth-century chess idea.

title: Morphy's Open Lines
text: Paul Morphy became famous for rapid development, open lines, and coordinated attacks. His best games look effortless because his pieces enter play with purpose. The deeper lesson is not to attack at random. First mobilize the whole force, protect the king, and act when the position supports action.
context: A strategic introduction to nineteenth-century master Paul Morphy.
vocabulary: mobilize: prepare and bring into action

title: Capablanca's Clarity
text: José Raúl Capablanca was admired for clear positions and precise endgame play. His moves often seemed simple only because he understood which complications were unnecessary. Simplicity in chess does not mean shallow thought. It means finding a move that solves several problems without creating avoidable weaknesses.
context: A profile of the Cuban world chess champion.
vocabulary: complication: a difficult combination of possibilities

title: Machines Learn the Board
text: Early chess programs relied heavily on human-written rules and searches through possible moves. Modern systems can also learn patterns from enormous sets of games or from playing themselves. Computers calculate brilliantly, but people still choose why to play: for competition, beauty, friendship, study, or delight.
context: A simplified history of computer chess without product endorsements.
